About the question text

Each NCERT question is shown in full above its solution, with its textbook location. The solutions are our own. This chapter has no intext questions; the three exercises have 19 numbered questions and 49 parts, and every part is solved separately below.

How every solution is laid out: Given / Asked → Concept used (and why it applies here) → Steps, one per line, with the reason in words → Check → ✅ Final answer → Common trap. Every proof starts from one side, makes one change per line (the move used is named), and ends "= RHS. Hence proved." (Topic 6).

Exercise 8.1

Exercise 8.1, Q1 (i)sin⁡A\sin AsinA and cos⁡A\cos AcosA2 marks

In △ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm. Determine:
(i) sin⁡A\sin AsinA, cos⁡A\cos AcosA

Given: △ABC with ∠B=90°\angle B = 90°∠B=90°, AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm. Asked: sin⁡A\sin AsinA and cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

Concept used: Pythagoras for the hypotenuse, then SOH-CAH-TOA with the sides labelled from ∠A\angle A∠A (Topic 1). Why it applies: both ratios need the hypotenuse AC, which is not given.

  1. 1

    AC is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle at B). Add the squares of the other two sides.

    AC2=AB2+BC2AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2AC2=AB2+BC2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Substitute.

    AC2=242+72=576+49AC^2 = 24^2 + 7^2 = 576 + 49AC2=242+72=576+49Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Add.

    AC2=625AC^2 = 625AC2=625Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Take the square root.

    AC=25 cmAC = 25 \text{ cm}AC=25 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    From ∠A\angle A∠A: opposite = BC = 7, adjacent = AB = 24, hypotenuse = AC = 25.

    sin⁡A=BCAC=725\sin A = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{7}{25}sinA=ACBC​=257​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Cosine.

    cos⁡A=ABAC=2425\cos A = \dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{24}{25}cosA=ACAB​=2524​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: both values are less than 1 ✔; 72+242=2527^2 + 24^2 = 25^272+242=252 ✔.

  8. Answer sin⁡A=725\sin A = \dfrac{7}{25}sinA=257​, cos⁡A=2425\cos A = \dfrac{24}{25}cosA=2524​

    Common trap: Taking AB (24) as the opposite side of A because it is "the side you see first". AB touches A, so it is adjacent.
Exercise 8.1, Q1 (ii)sin⁡C\sin CsinC and cos⁡C\cos CcosC2 marks

In △ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm. Determine:
(ii) sin⁡C\sin CsinC, cos⁡C\cos CcosC

Given: the same triangle; AC = 25 cm from part (i). Asked: sin⁡C\sin CsinC and cos⁡C\cos CcosC.

Concept used: relabel the sides from ∠C\angle C∠C (Topic 1). Why it applies: opposite and adjacent swap when we move from A to C.

  1. 1

    From ∠C\angle C∠C: opposite = AB = 24, adjacent = BC = 7, hypotenuse = AC = 25.

  2. 2

    Sine.

    sin⁡C=ABAC=2425\sin C = \dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{24}{25}sinC=ACAB​=2524​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Cosine.

    cos⁡C=BCAC=725\cos C = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{7}{25}cosC=ACBC​=257​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: sin⁡C=cos⁡A\sin C = \cos AsinC=cosA and cos⁡C=sin⁡A\cos C = \sin AcosC=sinA, as expected when the two sides swap roles ✔.

  5. Answer sin⁡C=2425\sin C = \dfrac{24}{25}sinC=2524​, cos⁡C=725\cos C = \dfrac{7}{25}cosC=257​

    Common trap: Copying the answers of part (i). The angle has changed, so the labels change.
Exercise 8.1, Q2tan⁡P−cot⁡R\tan P - \cot RtanP−cotR2 marks

In Fig. 8.13, find tan⁡P−cot⁡R\tan P - \cot RtanP−cotR.
(Fig. 8.13: △PQR with a right angle at Q, PQ = 12 cm and PR = 13 cm.)

Given: ∠Q=90°\angle Q = 90°∠Q=90°, PQ = 12 cm, PR = 13 cm. Asked: tan⁡P−cot⁡R\tan P - \cot RtanP−cotR.

Concept used: Pythagoras for QR; tan and cot with the sides labelled from each angle (Topic 1). Why it applies: both ratios need QR.

  1. 1

    PR is the hypotenuse; QR is a shorter side, so subtract.

    QR2=PR2−PQ2=132−122QR^2 = PR^2 - PQ^2 = 13^2 - 12^2QR2=PR2−PQ2=132−122Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Square and subtract.

    QR2=169−144=25QR^2 = 169 - 144 = 25QR2=169−144=25Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Take the square root.

    QR=5 cmQR = 5 \text{ cm}QR=5 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    From ∠P\angle P∠P: opposite = QR, adjacent = PQ.

    tan⁡P=QRPQ=512\tan P = \dfrac{QR}{PQ} = \dfrac{5}{12}tanP=PQQR​=125​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    From ∠R\angle R∠R: adjacent = QR, opposite = PQ. Cot is adjacent over opposite.

    cot⁡R=QRPQ=512\cot R = \dfrac{QR}{PQ} = \dfrac{5}{12}cotR=PQQR​=125​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract.

    tan⁡P−cot⁡R=512−512=0\tan P - \cot R = \dfrac{5}{12} - \dfrac{5}{12} = 0tanP−cotR=125​−125​=0Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: tan⁡P\tan PtanP and cot⁡R\cot RcotR use the same two sides in the same order, so they must be equal ✔.

  8. Answer tan⁡P−cot⁡R=0\tan P - \cot R = 0tanP−cotR=0

    Common trap: Writing cot⁡R=125\cot R = \dfrac{12}{5}cotR=512​ — labelling from P instead of R. From R, the side PQ is opposite.
Exercise 8.1, Q3Given sin⁡A=34\sin A = \dfrac{3}{4}sinA=43​2 marks

If sin⁡A=34\sin A = \dfrac{3}{4}sinA=43​, calculate cos⁡A\cos AcosA and tan⁡A\tan AtanA.

Given: sin⁡A=34\sin A = \dfrac{3}{4}sinA=43​. Asked: cos⁡A\cos AcosA and tan⁡A\tan AtanA.

Concept used: the five-step method of Topic 3 (ratio as sides → Pythagoras → read off). Why it applies: one ratio is given.

  1. 1

    sin⁡A=oppositehypotenuse=34\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{3}{4}sinA=hypotenuseopposite​=43​. In △ABC right-angled at B, take BC = 3k3k3k and AC = 4k4k4k (k>0k > 0k>0).

  2. 2

    AB is a shorter side, so subtract.

    AB2=(4k)2−(3k)2=16k2−9k2AB^2 = (4k)^2 - (3k)^2 = 16k^2 - 9k^2AB2=(4k)2−(3k)2=16k2−9k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Simplify.

    AB2=7k2AB^2 = 7k^2AB2=7k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Take the square root.

    AB=7 kAB = \sqrt{7}\,kAB=7​kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Cosine.

    cos⁡A=ABAC=7 k4k=74\cos A = \dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}\,k}{4k} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}cosA=ACAB​=4k7​k​=47​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Tangent.

    tan⁡A=BCAB=3k7 k=37\tan A = \dfrac{BC}{AB} = \dfrac{3k}{\sqrt{7}\,k} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}}tanA=ABBC​=7​k3k​=7​3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Rationalise (optional).

    tan⁡A=377\tan A = \dfrac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}tanA=737​​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Check: (34)2+(74)2=916+716=1\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{16} + \dfrac{7}{16} = 1(43​)2+(47​​)2=169​+167​=1 ✔.

  9. Answer cos⁡A=74\cos A = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}cosA=47​​, tan⁡A=37=377\tan A = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}tanA=7​3​=737​​

    Common trap: Adding in step 2 (9k2+16k2=25k29k^2 + 16k^2 = 25k^29k2+16k2=25k2, giving 5). The unknown is a shorter side, so subtract.
Exercise 8.1, Q4Given 15cot⁡A=815 \cot A = 815cotA=82 marks

Given 15cot⁡A=815\cot A = 815cotA=8, find sin⁡A\sin AsinA and sec⁡A\sec AsecA.

Given: 15cot⁡A=815\cot A = 815cotA=8. Asked: sin⁡A\sin AsinA and sec⁡A\sec AsecA.

Concept used: rewrite as cot⁡A=815\cot A = \dfrac{8}{15}cotA=158​, then the five-step method (Topic 3). Why it applies: one ratio is given.

  1. 1

    Divide both sides by 15.

    cot⁡A=815\cot A = \dfrac{8}{15}cotA=158​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    cot⁡A=adjacentopposite\cot A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}}cotA=oppositeadjacent​. Take adjacent AB =8k= 8k=8k and opposite BC =15k= 15k=15k.

  3. 3

    The hypotenuse: add the squares.

    AC2=(8k)2+(15k)2=64k2+225k2AC^2 = (8k)^2 + (15k)^2 = 64k^2 + 225k^2AC2=(8k)2+(15k)2=64k2+225k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Add.

    AC2=289k2AC^2 = 289k^2AC2=289k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Take the square root.

    AC=17kAC = 17kAC=17kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Sine.

    sin⁡A=BCAC=1517\sin A = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{15}{17}sinA=ACBC​=1715​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Secant is hypotenuse over adjacent.

    sec⁡A=ACAB=178\sec A = \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{17}{8}secA=ABAC​=817​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Check: 8, 15, 17 is a Pythagorean triple ✔; sec⁡A>1\sec A > 1secA>1 ✔.

  9. Answer sin⁡A=1517\sin A = \dfrac{15}{17}sinA=1715​, sec⁡A=178\sec A = \dfrac{17}{8}secA=817​

    Common trap: Treating 815\dfrac{8}{15}158​ as opposite over adjacent (that is tan). In cot the adjacent side is on top, which gives the wrong sin⁡A=817\sin A = \dfrac{8}{17}sinA=178​.
Exercise 8.1, Q5Given sec⁡θ=1312\sec\theta = \dfrac{13}{12}secθ=1213​3 marks

Given sec⁡θ=1312\sec\theta = \dfrac{13}{12}secθ=1213​, calculate all other trigonometric ratios.

Given: sec⁡θ=1312\sec\theta = \dfrac{13}{12}secθ=1213​. Asked: the other five ratios.

Concept used: sec⁡θ=hypotenuseadjacent\sec\theta = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent}}secθ=adjacenthypotenuse​; the five-step method (Topic 3). Why it applies: one ratio is given.

  1. 1

    Take hypotenuse =13k= 13k=13k and adjacent =12k= 12k=12k.

  2. 2

    The opposite side is shorter, so subtract.

    opp2=(13k)2−(12k)2=169k2−144k2\text{opp}^2 = (13k)^2 - (12k)^2 = 169k^2 - 144k^2opp2=(13k)2−(12k)2=169k2−144k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Subtract.

    opp2=25k2\text{opp}^2 = 25k^2opp2=25k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Take the square root.

    opp=5k\text{opp} = 5kopp=5kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Sine, cosine, tangent.

    sin⁡θ=513,cos⁡θ=1213,tan⁡θ=512\sin\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{12}sinθ=135​,cosθ=1312​,tanθ=125​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Cosecant and cotangent (reciprocals of sine and tangent).

    cosec⁡θ=135,cot⁡θ=125\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{13}{5}, \qquad \cot\theta = \dfrac{12}{5}cosecθ=513​,cotθ=512​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: cos⁡θ=1213\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}cosθ=1312​ is the reciprocal of sec⁡θ=1312\sec\theta = \dfrac{13}{12}secθ=1213​ ✔. 5, 12, 13 is a triple ✔.

  8. Answer sin⁡θ=513\sin\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}sinθ=135​, cos⁡θ=1213\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}cosθ=1312​, tan⁡θ=512\tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{12}tanθ=125​, cosec⁡θ=135\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{13}{5}cosecθ=513​, cot⁡θ=125\cot\theta = \dfrac{12}{5}cotθ=512​

    Common trap: Reading sec as "hypotenuse over opposite" (that is cosec), which swaps sin and cos in the answer.
Exercise 8.1, Q6If cos⁡A=cos⁡B\cos A = \cos BcosA=cosB, then ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B3 marks

If ∠A\angle A∠A and ∠B\angle B∠B are acute angles such that cos⁡A=cos⁡B\cos A = \cos BcosA=cosB, then show that ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B.

Given: acute angles A and B with cos⁡A=cos⁡B\cos A = \cos BcosA=cosB. To show: ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B.

Concept used: put each angle in its own right triangle; equal ratios of sides make the triangles similar (SSS similarity, Chapter 6). Why it applies: a trigonometric ratio fixes the shape of the triangle (Topic 1).

  1. Statement Reason
    1. Draw right △AMN with ∠M=90°\angle M = 90°∠M=90° and acute angle A, and right △BPQ with ∠P=90°\angle P = 90°∠P=90° and acute angle B. Any acute angle can be placed in a right triangle
    2. cos⁡A=AMAN\cos A = \dfrac{AM}{AN}cosA=ANAM​ and cos⁡B=BPBQ\cos B = \dfrac{BP}{BQ}cosB=BQBP​ Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse
    3. AMAN=BPBQ=k\dfrac{AM}{AN} = \dfrac{BP}{BQ} = kANAM​=BQBP​=k (say) Given cos⁡A=cos⁡B\cos A = \cos BcosA=cosB
    4. AM=k⋅ANAM = k \cdot ANAM=k⋅AN and BP=k⋅BQBP = k \cdot BQBP=k⋅BQ Multiply out step 3
    5. MN=AN2−AM2=AN2−k2AN2=AN1−k2MN = \sqrt{AN^2 - AM^2} = \sqrt{AN^2 - k^2 AN^2} = AN\sqrt{1 - k^2}MN=AN2−AM2​=AN2−k2AN2​=AN1−k2​ Pythagoras in △AMN, then step 4
    6. PQ=BQ2−BP2=BQ2−k2BQ2=BQ1−k2PQ = \sqrt{BQ^2 - BP^2} = \sqrt{BQ^2 - k^2 BQ^2} = BQ\sqrt{1 - k^2}PQ=BQ2−BP2​=BQ2−k2BQ2​=BQ1−k2​ Pythagoras in △BPQ, then step 4
    7. MNPQ=AN1−k2BQ1−k2=ANBQ\dfrac{MN}{PQ} = \dfrac{AN\sqrt{1 - k^2}}{BQ\sqrt{1 - k^2}} = \dfrac{AN}{BQ}PQMN​=BQ1−k2​AN1−k2​​=BQAN​ Divide step 5 by step 6
    8. AMBP=k⋅ANk⋅BQ=ANBQ\dfrac{AM}{BP} = \dfrac{k \cdot AN}{k \cdot BQ} = \dfrac{AN}{BQ}BPAM​=k⋅BQk⋅AN​=BQAN​ Divide the two parts of step 4
    9. AMBP=ANBQ=MNPQ\dfrac{AM}{BP} = \dfrac{AN}{BQ} = \dfrac{MN}{PQ}BPAM​=BQAN​=PQMN​ Steps 7 and 8
    10. △AMN ~ △BPQ SSS similarity: all three pairs of sides are in the same ratio
    11. ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B Corresponding angles of similar triangles are equal. Hence shown.

  2. Check (special case): if A and B are the two acute angles of one right triangle ABC (right angle at C), then cos⁡A=ACAB\cos A = \dfrac{AC}{AB}cosA=ABAC​ and cos⁡B=BCAB\cos B = \dfrac{BC}{AB}cosB=ABBC​; equal cosines give AC = BC, so the triangle is isosceles and ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B (both 45°). The general proof above covers every case.

  3. Answer Equal cosines make the two right triangles similar, so ∠A=∠B\angle A = \angle B∠A=∠B.

    Common trap: Proving only the special case (A and B in the same triangle). The question allows A and B to come from different triangles.
Exercise 8.1, Q7 (i)Evaluate with cot⁡θ=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=87​2 marks

If cot⁡θ=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=87​, evaluate:
(i) (1+sin⁡θ)(1−sin⁡θ)(1+cos⁡θ)(1−cos⁡θ)\dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 + \cos\theta)(1 - \cos\theta)}(1+cosθ)(1−cosθ)(1+sinθ)(1−sinθ)​

Given: cot⁡θ=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=87​. Asked: the value of the expression.

Concept used: (a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2(a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2 to simplify, then find sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ and cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ from cot⁡θ\cot\thetacotθ (Topic 3). Why it applies: the brackets multiply out to 1−sin⁡2θ1 - \sin^2\theta1−sin2θ and 1−cos⁡2θ1 - \cos^2\theta1−cos2θ.

  1. 1

    Multiply out the top and bottom using (a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2(a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2.

    1−sin⁡2θ1−cos⁡2θ\dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{1 - \cos^2\theta}1−cos2θ1−sin2θ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Find the ratios: cot⁡θ=adjopp=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}} = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=oppadj​=87​, so adjacent =7k= 7k=7k, opposite =8k= 8k=8k.

  3. 3

    Hypotenuse: add the squares.

    hyp2=49k2+64k2=113k2\text{hyp}^2 = 49k^2 + 64k^2 = 113k^2hyp2=49k2+64k2=113k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Take the square root.

    hyp=113 k\text{hyp} = \sqrt{113}\,khyp=113​kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Square the sine and cosine.

    sin⁡2θ=64113,cos⁡2θ=49113\sin^2\theta = \dfrac{64}{113}, \qquad \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{49}{113}sin2θ=11364​,cos2θ=11349​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Work out the top: 1−641131 - \dfrac{64}{113}1−11364​.

    1−sin⁡2θ=491131 - \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{49}{113}1−sin2θ=11349​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Work out the bottom: 1−491131 - \dfrac{49}{113}1−11349​.

    1−cos⁡2θ=641131 - \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{64}{113}1−cos2θ=11364​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Divide (the 113s cancel).

      49113    64113  =4964\dfrac{\;\dfrac{49}{113}\;}{\;\dfrac{64}{113}\;} = \dfrac{49}{64}11364​11349​​=6449​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: 1−sin⁡2θ1−cos⁡2θ=cos⁡2θsin⁡2θ=cot⁡2θ=(78)2=4964\dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{1 - \cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \cot^2\theta = \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{64}1−cos2θ1−sin2θ​=sin2θcos2θ​=cot2θ=(87​)2=6449​ (using Topic 5) ✔.

  10. Answer 4964\dfrac{49}{64}6449​

    Common trap: Multiplying out (1+sin⁡θ)(1−sin⁡θ)(1 + \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)(1+sinθ)(1−sinθ) as 1−sin⁡θ1 - \sin\theta1−sinθ — the square is missing.
Exercise 8.1, Q7 (ii)cot⁡2θ\cot^2\thetacot2θ1 mark

If cot⁡θ=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=87​, evaluate:
(ii) cot⁡2θ\cot^2\thetacot2θ

Given: cot⁡θ=78\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}cotθ=87​. Asked: cot⁡2θ\cot^2\thetacot2θ.

Concept used: cot⁡2θ\cot^2\thetacot2θ means (cot⁡θ)2(\cot\theta)^2(cotθ)2 (Topic 1). Why it applies: square the given fraction.

  1. 1

    Square the fraction — top and bottom.

    cot⁡2θ=(78)2=4964\cot^2\theta = \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{64}cot2θ=(87​)2=6449​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  2. Check: it equals the answer to part (i), as the check there showed it must ✔.

  3. Answer cot⁡2θ=4964\cot^2\theta = \dfrac{49}{64}cot2θ=6449​

    Common trap: (78)2=498\left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{8}(87​)2=849​ — squaring only the top.
Exercise 8.1, Q8Check an equality when 3cot⁡A=43\cot A = 43cotA=43 marks

If 3cot⁡A=43 \cot A = 43cotA=4, check whether 1−tan⁡2A1+tan⁡2A=cos⁡2A−sin⁡2A\dfrac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A} = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A1+tan2A1−tan2A​=cos2A−sin2A or not.

Given: 3cot⁡A=43\cot A = 43cotA=4. Asked: whether the two expressions are equal.

Concept used: find all ratios from one (Topic 3), then evaluate both sides separately. Why it applies: we need tan⁡A\tan AtanA, sin⁡A\sin AsinA and cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

  1. 1

    cot⁡A=43\cot A = \dfrac{4}{3}cotA=34​, so adjacent =4k= 4k=4k and opposite =3k= 3k=3k.

  2. 2

    Hypotenuse: add the squares.

    hyp2=16k2+9k2=25k2\text{hyp}^2 = 16k^2 + 9k^2 = 25k^2hyp2=16k2+9k2=25k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Take the square root.

    hyp=5k\text{hyp} = 5khyp=5kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    The ratios needed.

    tan⁡A=34,sin⁡A=35,cos⁡A=45\tan A = \dfrac{3}{4}, \qquad \sin A = \dfrac{3}{5}, \qquad \cos A = \dfrac{4}{5}tanA=43​,sinA=53​,cosA=54​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Left side: square tan⁡A\tan AtanA and write 1 as 1616\dfrac{16}{16}1616​.

    1−tan⁡2A1+tan⁡2A=1−9161+916=  716    2516  \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A} = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{9}{16}}{1 + \dfrac{9}{16}} = \dfrac{\;\dfrac{7}{16}\;}{\;\dfrac{25}{16}\;}1+tan2A1−tan2A​=1+169​1−169​​=1625​167​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    The 16s cancel.

    =725= \dfrac{7}{25}=257​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Right side.

    cos⁡2A−sin⁡2A=1625−925\cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = \dfrac{16}{25} - \dfrac{9}{25}cos2A−sin2A=2516​−259​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract.

    =725= \dfrac{7}{25}=257​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: both sides equal 725\dfrac{7}{25}257​ ✔.

  10. Answer Yes, 1−tan⁡2A1+tan⁡2A=cos⁡2A−sin⁡2A\dfrac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A} = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A1+tan2A1−tan2A​=cos2A−sin2A (both equal 725\dfrac{7}{25}257​).

    Common trap: Using tan⁡A=43\tan A = \dfrac{4}{3}tanA=34​ (copying the cot value). Tan is the reciprocal of cot: tan⁡A=34\tan A = \dfrac{3}{4}tanA=43​. With 43\dfrac{4}{3}34​ the left side would come out as −725-\dfrac{7}{25}−257​.
Exercise 8.1, Q9 (i)sin⁡Acos⁡C+cos⁡Asin⁡C\sin A \cos C + \cos A \sin CsinAcosC+cosAsinC2 marks

In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan⁡A=13\tan A = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tanA=3​1​, find the value of:
(i) sin⁡Acos⁡C+cos⁡Asin⁡C\sin A\cos C + \cos A\sin CsinAcosC+cosAsinC

Given: ∠B=90°\angle B = 90°∠B=90°, tan⁡A=13\tan A = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tanA=3​1​. Asked: sin⁡Acos⁡C+cos⁡Asin⁡C\sin A\cos C + \cos A\sin CsinAcosC+cosAsinC.

Concept used: find the sides from tan⁡A\tan AtanA, then label from A and from C (Topic 1, Topic 3). Why it applies: the expression uses ratios of both acute angles.

  1. 1

    tan⁡A=BCAB=13\tan A = \dfrac{BC}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tanA=ABBC​=3​1​: take BC =k= k=k and AB =3 k= \sqrt{3}\,k=3​k.

  2. 2

    Hypotenuse AC: add the squares.

    AC2=k2+3k2=4k2AC^2 = k^2 + 3k^2 = 4k^2AC2=k2+3k2=4k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Take the square root.

    AC=2kAC = 2kAC=2kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Ratios of A (opposite BC, adjacent AB).

    sin⁡A=12,cos⁡A=32\sin A = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \cos A = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}sinA=21​,cosA=23​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Ratios of C (opposite AB, adjacent BC).

    sin⁡C=32,cos⁡C=12\sin C = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad \cos C = \dfrac{1}{2}sinC=23​​,cosC=21​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Substitute.

    sin⁡Acos⁡C+cos⁡Asin⁡C=12×12+32×32\sin A\cos C + \cos A\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}sinAcosC+cosAsinC=21​×21​+23​​×23​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Multiply.

    =14+34= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4}=41​+43​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Add.

    =1= 1=1Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: here A = 30° and C = 60° (Topic 4), and sin⁡30°cos⁡60°+cos⁡30°sin⁡60°=14+34=1\sin 30°\cos 60° + \cos 30°\sin 60° = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1sin30°cos60°+cos30°sin60°=41​+43​=1 ✔.

  10. Answer 111

    Common trap: Using the same values for C as for A. From C the opposite and adjacent sides swap.

Exercise 8.1, Q10PR + QR = 25 cm, PQ = 5 cm3 marks

In △PQR\triangle PQR△PQR, right-angled at Q, PR + QR = 25 cm and PQ = 5 cm. Determine the values of sin⁡P\sin PsinP, cos⁡P\cos PcosP and tan⁡P\tan PtanP.

Given: ∠Q=90°\angle Q = 90°∠Q=90°, PR + QR = 25 cm, PQ = 5 cm. Asked: sin⁡P\sin PsinP, cos⁡P\cos PcosP, tan⁡P\tan PtanP.

Concept used: let one unknown side be xxx, use Pythagoras to form an equation (Topic 2), then SOH-CAH-TOA. Why it applies: we know only the sum of two sides.

  1. 1

    Let QR =x= x=x cm. Then PR =(25−x)= (25 - x)=(25−x) cm.

  2. 2

    Pythagoras (PR is the hypotenuse).

    PR2=PQ2+QR2PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2PR2=PQ2+QR2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute.

    (25−x)2=52+x2(25 - x)^2 = 5^2 + x^2(25−x)2=52+x2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand the left side using (a−b)2=a2−2ab+b2(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2(a−b)2=a2−2ab+b2.

    625−50x+x2=25+x2625 - 50x + x^2 = 25 + x^2625−50x+x2=25+x2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract x2x^2x2 from both sides.

    625−50x=25625 - 50x = 25625−50x=25Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract 625 from both sides.

    −50x=−600-50x = -600−50x=−600Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by −50-50−50.

    x=12x = 12x=12Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    So QR = 12 cm and PR = 25 − 12 = 13 cm.

  9. 9

    From ∠P\angle P∠P: opposite = QR = 12, adjacent = PQ = 5, hypotenuse = PR = 13.

    sin⁡P=1213,cos⁡P=513,tan⁡P=125\sin P = \dfrac{12}{13}, \qquad \cos P = \dfrac{5}{13}, \qquad \tan P = \dfrac{12}{5}sinP=1312​,cosP=135​,tanP=512​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  10. Check: 52+122=25+144=169=1325^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^252+122=25+144=169=132 ✔ and 13+12=2513 + 12 = 2513+12=25 ✔.

  11. Answer sin⁡P=1213\sin P = \dfrac{12}{13}sinP=1312​, cos⁡P=513\cos P = \dfrac{5}{13}cosP=135​, tan⁡P=125\tan P = \dfrac{12}{5}tanP=512​

    Common trap: Expanding (25−x)2(25 - x)^2(25−x)2 as 625−x2625 - x^2625−x2, which loses the −50x-50x−50x term. Use (a−b)2=a2−2ab+b2(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2(a−b)2=a2−2ab+b2.
Exercise 8.1, Q11 (i)"tan A is always less than 1"1 mark

State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(i) The value of tan⁡A\tan AtanA is always less than 1.

Given: the statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: tan⁡A=oppositeadjacent\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}tanA=adjacentopposite​ compares the two shorter sides (Topic 1). Why it applies: either of these sides can be the longer one.

  1. 1

    A counter-example is enough to show the statement is false.

  2. 2

    In a right triangle with opposite side 12 cm and adjacent side 5 cm, tan⁡A=125\tan A = \dfrac{12}{5}tanA=512​, which is more than 1.

  3. 3

    Also, from the table, tan⁡60°=3≈1.73>1\tan 60° = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 > 1tan60°=3​≈1.73>1.

  4. Answer False. For example, tan⁡60°=3>1\tan 60° = \sqrt{3} > 1tan60°=3​>1.

    Common trap: Mixing up tan with sin and cos, which are less than 1 for acute angles.
Exercise 8.1, Q11 (ii)"sec⁡A=125\sec A = \dfrac{12}{5}secA=512​ for some A"1 mark

State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(ii) sec⁡A=125\sec A = \dfrac{12}{5}secA=512​ for some value of angle A.

Given: the statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: sec⁡A=hypotenuseadjacent\sec A = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent}}secA=adjacenthypotenuse​, which is greater than 1 for acute A (Topic 3). Why it applies: we only need a triangle with hypotenuse 12 and adjacent side 5.

  1. 1

    125=2.4>1\dfrac{12}{5} = 2.4 > 1512​=2.4>1, so the value is possible for a secant.

  2. 2

    Construct it: hypotenuse 12 cm, adjacent side 5 cm. The third side is 144−25=119\sqrt{144 - 25} = \sqrt{119}144−25​=119​ cm, a real length.

  3. 3

    In this triangle sec⁡A=125\sec A = \dfrac{12}{5}secA=512​.

  4. Answer True. A right triangle with hypotenuse 12 and adjacent side 5 (opposite side 119\sqrt{119}119​) has sec⁡A=125\sec A = \dfrac{12}{5}secA=512​.

    Common trap: Saying "false because it is more than 1". That rule is for sin and cos; sec is always at least 1.
Exercise 8.1, Q11 (iii)"cos A is the abbreviation for cosecant"1 mark

State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(iii) cos⁡A\cos AcosA is the abbreviation used for the cosecant of angle A.

Given: the statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: the names of the six ratios (Topic 1). Why it applies: the statement is about notation.

  1. 1

    "cos A" stands for the cosine of A (adjacenthypotenuse\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}hypotenuseadjacent​).

  2. 2

    The cosecant of A is written "cosec⁡A\operatorname{cosec} AcosecA" (hypotenuseopposite\dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{opposite}}oppositehypotenuse​).

  3. Answer False. cos A is the cosine of A; the cosecant is written cosec⁡A\operatorname{cosec} AcosecA.

Exercise 8.1, Q11 (iv)"cot A is the product of cot and A"1 mark

State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(iv) cot⁡A\cot AcotA is the product of cot and A.

Given: the statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: a ratio and its angle form one symbol (Topic 1). Why it applies: "cot" alone has no value.

  1. 1

    "cot A" means the cotangent of angle A — one number, adjacentopposite\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}}oppositeadjacent​.

  2. 2

    "cot" on its own is not a number, so it cannot be multiplied by A.

  3. Answer False. cot A is one symbol, the cotangent of angle A; it is not "cot × A".

    Common trap: Cancelling the A in expressions like cot⁡AA\dfrac{\cot A}{A}AcotA​. You can never separate a ratio from its angle.
Exercise 8.1, Q11 (v)"sin⁡θ=43\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}sinθ=34​ for some θ"1 mark

State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(v) sin⁡θ=43\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}sinθ=34​ for some angle θ\thetaθ.

Given: the statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: sin⁡θ=oppositehypotenuse\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}sinθ=hypotenuseopposite​ and the hypotenuse is the longest side (Topic 1). Why it applies: 43>1\dfrac{4}{3} > 134​>1.

  1. 1

    sin⁡θ=43\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}sinθ=34​ would need the opposite side to be longer than the hypotenuse.

  2. 2

    The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle, so this is impossible. In fact sin⁡θ≤1\sin\theta \leq 1sinθ≤1 for every angle θ\thetaθ from 0° to 90°.

  3. Answer False. sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ can never exceed 1, but 43>1\dfrac{4}{3} > 134​>1.

  4. 4

    1≠1+321 \neq \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}1=21+3​​.

  5. Answer False. For A = 30°, B = 60°: LHS = 1 but RHS =1+32= \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}=21+3​​.

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 1 (sin and cos), Move 4 (sin⁡2θ=1−cos⁡2θ\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\thetasin2θ=1−cos2θ), Move 5 (factorise 1−cos⁡2θ1 - \cos^2\theta1−cos2θ and cancel). Why it applies: the RHS has only cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ, so we need to remove sin⁡2θ\sin^2\thetasin2θ.

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=(cosec⁡θ−cot⁡θ)2\text{LHS} = (\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta)^2LHS=(cosecθ−cotθ)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 1: change to sin and cos.

    =(1sin⁡θ−cos⁡θsin⁡θ)2= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2=(sinθ1​−sinθcosθ​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Same denominator — combine inside the bracket.

    =(1−cos⁡θsin⁡θ)2= \left(\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2=(sinθ1−cosθ​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Square the top and the bottom.

    =(1−cos⁡θ)2sin⁡2θ= \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}=sin2θ(1−cosθ)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: sin⁡2θ=1−cos⁡2θ\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\thetasin2θ=1−cos2θ.

    =(1−cos⁡θ)21−cos⁡2θ= \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{1 - \cos^2\theta}=1−cos2θ(1−cosθ)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: factorise the bottom, 1−cos⁡2θ=(1−cos⁡θ)(1+cos⁡θ)1 - \cos^2\theta = (1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)1−cos2θ=(1−cosθ)(1+cosθ).

    =(1−cos⁡θ)(1−cos⁡θ)(1−cos⁡θ)(1+cos⁡θ)= \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)(1 - \cos\theta)}{(1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)}=(1−cosθ)(1+cosθ)(1−cosθ)(1−cosθ)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cancel the common factor (1−cos⁡θ)(1 - \cos\theta)(1−cosθ).

    =1−cos⁡θ1+cos⁡θ=RHS= \dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} = \text{RHS}=1+cosθ1−cosθ​=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Hence proved.

    Check: at θ = 60°: LHS =(23−13)2=13= \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}=(3​2​−3​1​)2=31​; RHS =1−121+12=13= \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}=1+21​1−21​​=31​ ✔.

    =sc×ss−c+cs×cc−s= \dfrac{s}{c} \times \dfrac{s}{s - c} + \dfrac{c}{s} \times \dfrac{c}{c - s}=cs​×s−cs​+sc​×c−sc​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Multiply out each fraction.

  6. 5

    Write c−s=−(s−c)c - s = -(s - c)c−s=−(s−c) so both fractions have the factor (s−c)(s - c)(s−c).

    =s2c(s−c)−c2s(s−c)= \dfrac{s^2}{c(s - c)} - \dfrac{c^2}{s(s - c)}=c(s−c)s2​−s(s−c)c2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 6

    Move 2: LCM sc(s−c)sc(s - c)sc(s−c).

    =s3−c3sc(s−c)= \dfrac{s^3 - c^3}{sc(s - c)}=sc(s−c)s3−c3​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    =(s−c)(s2+sc+c2)sc(s−c)= \dfrac{(s - c)(s^2 + sc + c^2)}{sc(s - c)}=sc(s−c)(s−c)(s2+sc+c2)​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Move 4: s2+c2=1s^2 + c^2 = 1s2+c2=1.

    Move 1 in reverse: 1sin⁡θcos⁡θ=cosec⁡θsec⁡θ\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\thetasinθcosθ1​=cosecθsecθ.

Check: at θ = 60°: LHS =31−13+131−3=33−1−13(3−1)=33−13(3−1)= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} + \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{1 - \sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3} - 1} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3} - 1)} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3} - 1}{\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3} - 1)}=1−3​1​3​​+1−3​3​1​​=3​−13​−3​(3​−1)1​=3​(3​−1)33​−1​, and RHS =1+2×23=1+43= 1 + 2 \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 1 + \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}=1+2×3​2​=1+3​4​; both ≈3.309\approx 3.309≈3.309 ✔.

    Common trap: In step 5, forgetting to change the sign when writing c−sc - sc−s as −(s−c)-(s - c)−(s−c). Without the minus sign the top becomes s3+c3s^3 + c^3s3+c3, which does not factorise with (s−c)(s - c)(s−c).

Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.

[Hint: Simplify LHS and RHS separately]

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: simplify each side separately to the same expression. LHS: Move 1. RHS: Move 4 and Move 5. Why it applies: the hint asks for it, and both sides reduce to 1+cos⁡A1 + \cos A1+cosA.

  1. 1

    Left-hand side

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=1+sec⁡Asec⁡A\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1 + \sec A}{\sec A}LHS=secA1+secA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Split the fraction.

    =1sec⁡A+sec⁡Asec⁡A= \dfrac{1}{\sec A} + \dfrac{\sec A}{\sec A}=secA1​+secAsecA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    1sec⁡A=cos⁡A\dfrac{1}{\sec A} = \cos AsecA1​=cosA and sec⁡Asec⁡A=1\dfrac{\sec A}{\sec A} = 1secAsecA​=1.

    =cos⁡A+1= \cos A + 1=cosA+1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Right-hand side

    Start from the RHS.

    RHS=sin⁡2A1−cos⁡A\text{RHS} = \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{1 - \cos A}RHS=1−cosAsin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: sin⁡2A=1−cos⁡2A\sin^2 A = 1 - \cos^2 Asin2A=1−cos2A.

    =1−cos⁡2A1−cos⁡A= \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 A}{1 - \cos A}=1−cosA1−cos2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: factorise the top.

    =(1−cos⁡A)(1+cos⁡A)1−cos⁡A= \dfrac{(1 - \cos A)(1 + \cos A)}{1 - \cos A}=1−cosA(1−cosA)(1+cosA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cancel (1−cos⁡A)(1 - \cos A)(1−cosA).

    =1+cos⁡A= 1 + \cos A=1+cosASwipe to see the whole equation →

    Conclusion: LHS =1+cos⁡A== 1 + \cos A ==1+cosA= RHS. Hence proved.

  8. Check: at A = 60°: LHS =1+22=32= \dfrac{1 + 2}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}=21+2​=23​; RHS =3412=32= \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{4}}{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2}=21​43​​=23​ ✔.

    Common trap: Cancelling sec⁡A\sec AsecA in 1+sec⁡Asec⁡A\dfrac{1 + \sec A}{\sec A}secA1+secA​ to get "1 + 1". sec⁡A\sec AsecA is not a factor of the whole top — split the fraction instead.

Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
(v) cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1=cosec⁡A+cot⁡A\dfrac{\cos A - \sin A + 1}{\cos A + \sin A - 1} = \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot AcosA+sinA−1cosA−sinA+1​=cosecA+cotA, using the identity cosec⁡2A=1+cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 Acosec2A=1+cot2A.

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS, using cosec⁡2A=1+cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 Acosec2A=1+cot2A.

Concept used: divide top and bottom by sin⁡A\sin AsinA to get cot and cosec; Move 4 (replace the 1 on top by cosec⁡2A−cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 Acosec2A−cot2A); Move 5 (factorise and cancel). Why it applies: the question asks for the cosec–cot identity, so we work in cot and cosec.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1\text{LHS} = \dfrac{\cos A - \sin A + 1}{\cos A + \sin A - 1}LHS=cosA+sinA−1cosA−sinA+1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Divide every term on top and bottom by sin⁡A\sin AsinA (this does not change the value): cos⁡Asin⁡A=cot⁡A\dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A} = \cot AsinAcosA​=cotA, 1sin⁡A=cosec⁡A\dfrac{1}{\sin A} = \operatorname{cosec} AsinA1​=cosecA.

    =cot⁡A−1+cosec⁡Acot⁡A+1−cosec⁡A= \dfrac{\cot A - 1 + \operatorname{cosec} A}{\cot A + 1 - \operatorname{cosec} A}=cotA+1−cosecAcotA−1+cosecA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Reorder the top to group (cot⁡A+cosec⁡A)(\cot A + \operatorname{cosec} A)(cotA+cosecA).

    =(cot⁡A+cosec⁡A)−1cot⁡A−cosec⁡A+1= \dfrac{(\cot A + \operatorname{cosec} A) - 1}{\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A + 1}=cotA−cosecA+1(cotA+cosecA)−1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 4: in the top, replace 1 by cosec⁡2A−cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 Acosec2A−cot2A (from cosec⁡2A=1+cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 Acosec2A=1+cot2A).

    =(cot⁡A+cosec⁡A)−(cosec⁡2A−cot⁡2A)cot⁡A−cosec⁡A+1= \dfrac{(\cot A + \operatorname{cosec} A) - (\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 A)}{\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A + 1}=cotA−cosecA+1(cotA+cosecA)−(cosec2A−cot2A)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Factorise the difference of squares: cosec⁡2A−cot⁡2A=(cosec⁡A+cot⁡A)(cosec⁡A−cot⁡A)\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 A = (\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)(\operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A)cosec2A−cot2A=(cosecA+cotA)(cosecA−cotA).

    =(cot⁡A+cosec⁡A)−(cosec⁡A+cot⁡A)(cosec⁡A−cot⁡A)cot⁡A−cosec⁡A+1= \dfrac{(\cot A + \operatorname{cosec} A) - (\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)(\operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A)}{\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A + 1}=cotA−cosecA+1(cotA+cosecA)−(cosecA+cotA)(cosecA−cotA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: take out the common factor (cosec⁡A+cot⁡A)(\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)(cosecA+cotA).

    =(cosec⁡A+cot⁡A) [1−(cosec⁡A−cot⁡A)]cot⁡A−cosec⁡A+1= \dfrac{(\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)\,[1 - (\operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A)]}{\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A + 1}=cotA−cosecA+1(cosecA+cotA)[1−(cosecA−cotA)]​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Open the square bracket: 1−cosec⁡A+cot⁡A1 - \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A1−cosecA+cotA.

    =(cosec⁡A+cot⁡A)(1−cosec⁡A+cot⁡A)cot⁡A−cosec⁡A+1= \dfrac{(\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)(1 - \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)}{\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A + 1}=cotA−cosecA+1(cosecA+cotA)(1−cosecA+cotA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    The second bracket on top equals the whole bottom; cancel it.

    =cosec⁡A+cot⁡A=RHS= \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A = \text{RHS}=cosecA+cotA=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 60°: LHS =12−32+112+32−1=3−33−1=3= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 1}{\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1} = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3} - 1} = \sqrt{3}=21​+23​​−121​−23​​+1​=3​−13−3​​=3​; RHS =23+13=33=3= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}=3​2​+3​1​=3​3​=3​ ✔.

    Alternative (optional): multiply top and bottom by (cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)(cosA+sinA+1); the bottom becomes (cos⁡A+sin⁡A)2−1=2sin⁡Acos⁡A(\cos A + \sin A)^2 - 1 = 2\sin A\cos A(cosA+sinA)2−1=2sinAcosA and the top becomes 2cos⁡A(1+cos⁡A)2\cos A(1 + \cos A)2cosA(1+cosA), giving 1+cos⁡Asin⁡A=cosec⁡A+cot⁡A\dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} = \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot AsinA1+cosA​=cosecA+cotA. (This is the method in the CBSE marking scheme for the same identity — see the sample-paper section.)

    Common trap: Replacing 1 by cosec⁡2A−cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 Acosec2A−cot2A in the bottom as well. Only the top needs it; the bottom is the bracket that cancels.

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 3 (multiply inside the root by the conjugate 1+sin⁡A1+sin⁡A\dfrac{1 + \sin A}{1 + \sin A}1+sinA1+sinA​), Move 4 (1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A), then split. Why it applies: the conjugate makes the bottom a perfect square, so the square root can be taken.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=1+sin⁡A1−sin⁡A\text{LHS} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \sin A}{1 - \sin A}}LHS=1−sinA1+sinA​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 3: multiply top and bottom inside the root by (1+sin⁡A)(1 + \sin A)(1+sinA).

    =(1+sin⁡A)(1+sin⁡A)(1−sin⁡A)(1+sin⁡A)= \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin A)(1 + \sin A)}{(1 - \sin A)(1 + \sin A)}}=(1−sinA)(1+sinA)(1+sinA)(1+sinA)​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Top: (1+sin⁡A)2(1 + \sin A)^2(1+sinA)2. Bottom: 1−sin⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A1−sin2A.

    =(1+sin⁡A)21−sin⁡2A= \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin A)^2}{1 - \sin^2 A}}=1−sin2A(1+sinA)2​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 4: 1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A.

    =(1+sin⁡A)2cos⁡2A= \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin A)^2}{\cos^2 A}}=cos2A(1+sinA)2​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Take the square root (both 1+sin⁡A1 + \sin A1+sinA and cos⁡A\cos AcosA are positive for acute A).

    =1+sin⁡Acos⁡A= \dfrac{1 + \sin A}{\cos A}=cosA1+sinA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Split into two fractions.

    =1cos⁡A+sin⁡Acos⁡A= \dfrac{1}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}=cosA1​+cosAsinA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Move 1 in reverse.

    =sec⁡A+tan⁡A=RHS= \sec A + \tan A = \text{RHS}=secA+tanA=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 30°: LHS =3212=3= \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{3}{2}}{\dfrac{1}{2}}} = \sqrt{3}=21​23​​​=3​; RHS =23+13=3= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}=3​2​+3​1​=3​ ✔.

    Common trap: Taking the square root of the top and bottom separately at step 1: 1+sin⁡A1−sin⁡A\dfrac{\sqrt{1 + \sin A}}{\sqrt{1 - \sin A}}1−sinA​1+sinA​​ does not simplify. Make perfect squares first.

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=(sin⁡A+cosec⁡A)2+(cos⁡A+sec⁡A)2\text{LHS} = (\sin A + \operatorname{cosec} A)^2 + (\cos A + \sec A)^2LHS=(sinA+cosecA)2+(cosA+secA)2Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Expand both squares.

    Reciprocal pairs: sin⁡Acosec⁡A=1\sin A\operatorname{cosec} A = 1sinAcosecA=1 and cos⁡Asec⁡A=1\cos A\sec A = 1cosAsecA=1.

    =sin⁡2A+2+cosec⁡2A+cos⁡2A+2+sec⁡2A= \sin^2 A + 2 + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A + \cos^2 A + 2 + \sec^2 A=sin2A+2+cosec2A+cos2A+2+sec2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Group: (sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A)+4+cosec⁡2A+sec⁡2A(\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A) + 4 + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A + \sec^2 A(sin2A+cos2A)+4+cosec2A+sec2A, and use sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A=1\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1sin2A+cos2A=1 (Move 4).

    =1+4+cosec⁡2A+sec⁡2A= 1 + 4 + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A + \sec^2 A=1+4+cosec2A+sec2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: cosec⁡2A=1+cot⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 Acosec2A=1+cot2A and sec⁡2A=1+tan⁡2A\sec^2 A = 1 + \tan^2 Asec2A=1+tan2A.

    =5+(1+cot⁡2A)+(1+tan⁡2A)= 5 + (1 + \cot^2 A) + (1 + \tan^2 A)=5+(1+cot2A)+(1+tan2A)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Add the numbers.

    =7+tan⁡2A+cot⁡2A=RHS= 7 + \tan^2 A + \cot^2 A = \text{RHS}=7+tan2A+cot2A=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 45°: LHS =(12+2)2×2=(32)2×2=9= (\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \sqrt{2})^2 \times 2 = \left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \times 2 = 9=(2​1​+2​)2×2=(2​3​)2×2=9; RHS =7+1+1=9= 7 + 1 + 1 = 9=7+1+1=9 ✔.

Concept used: simplify each side separately with Move 1 (sin and cos), Move 2 (LCM) and Move 4; both reduce to sin⁡Acos⁡A\sin A\cos AsinAcosA. Why it applies: the hint asks for it.

    Left-hand side

    Start from the LHS.

  2. 2

    Move 1.

    =(1sin⁡A−sin⁡A)(1cos⁡A−cos⁡A)= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin A} - \sin A\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos A} - \cos A\right)=(sinA1​−sinA)(cosA1​−cosA)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Move 2: combine each bracket.

    =1−sin⁡2Asin⁡A×1−cos⁡2Acos⁡A= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 A}{\sin A} \times \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 A}{\cos A}=sinA1−sin2A​×cosA1−cos2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 4: 1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A and 1−cos⁡2A=sin⁡2A1 - \cos^2 A = \sin^2 A1−cos2A=sin2A.

    =cos⁡2Asin⁡A×sin⁡2Acos⁡A= \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\sin A} \times \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos A}=sinAcos2A​×cosAsin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Cancel one sin⁡A\sin AsinA and one cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

    =sin⁡Acos⁡A= \sin A\cos A=sinAcosASwipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Right-hand side

    Start from the RHS.

    RHS=1tan⁡A+cot⁡A\text{RHS} = \dfrac{1}{\tan A + \cot A}RHS=tanA+cotA1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Move 1.

    =1sin⁡Acos⁡A+cos⁡Asin⁡A= \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}}=cosAsinA​+sinAcosA​1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Move 2: combine the bottom.

    =1  sin⁡2A+cos⁡2Asin⁡Acos⁡A  = \dfrac{1}{\;\dfrac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A\cos A}\;}=sinAcosAsin2A+cos2A​1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Move 4: sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A=1\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1sin2A+cos2A=1.

    =1  1sin⁡Acos⁡A  = \dfrac{1}{\;\dfrac{1}{\sin A\cos A}\;}=sinAcosA1​1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    One over a fraction is the fraction turned upside down.

    =sin⁡Acos⁡A= \sin A\cos A=sinAcosASwipe to see the whole equation →

    Conclusion: LHS =sin⁡Acos⁡A== \sin A\cos A ==sinAcosA= RHS. Hence proved.

  11. Check: at A = 30°: LHS =(2−12)(23−32)=32×123=34= \left(2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}=(2−21​)(3​2​−23​​)=23​×23​1​=43​​; sin⁡30°cos⁡30°=34\sin 30°\cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}sin30°cos30°=43​​ ✔.

    Common trap: Writing 1tan⁡A+cot⁡A=1tan⁡A+1cot⁡A\dfrac{1}{\tan A + \cot A} = \dfrac{1}{\tan A} + \dfrac{1}{\cot A}tanA+cotA1​=tanA1​+cotA1​. A fraction with a sum on the bottom does not split.
Exercise 8.3, Q4 (x)1+tan⁡2A1+cot⁡2A=(1−tan⁡A1−cot⁡A)2=tan⁡2A\dfrac{1 + \tan^2 A}{1 + \cot^2 A} = \left(\dfrac{1 - \tan A}{1 - \cot A}\right)^2 = \tan^2 A1+cot2A1+tan2A​=(1−cotA1−tanA​)2=tan2A3 marks

Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
(x) (1+tan⁡2A1+cot⁡2A)=(1−tan⁡A1−cot⁡A)2=tan⁡2A\left(\dfrac{1 + \tan^2 A}{1 + \cot^2 A}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1 - \tan A}{1 - \cot A}\right)^2 = \tan^2 A(1+cot2A1+tan2A​)=(1−cotA1−tanA​)2=tan2A

Given: a three-part identity. To prove: the first expression =tan⁡2A= \tan^2 A=tan2A and the second expression =tan⁡2A= \tan^2 A=tan2A.

Concept used: show that each of the first two expressions equals tan⁡2A\tan^2 Atan2A, working on one at a time. First: Move 4 then Move 1. Second: write cot⁡A=1tan⁡A\cot A = \dfrac{1}{\tan A}cotA=tanA1​ and simplify. Why it applies: if both equal tan⁡2A\tan^2 Atan2A, all three are equal.

  1. 1

    First expression

    Start from the first expression.

    1+tan⁡2A1+cot⁡2A\dfrac{1 + \tan^2 A}{1 + \cot^2 A}1+cot2A1+tan2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 4 on the top and bottom.

    =sec⁡2Acosec⁡2A= \dfrac{\sec^2 A}{\operatorname{cosec}^2 A}=cosec2Asec2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Move 1.

    =1cos⁡2A×sin⁡2A= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} \times \sin^2 A=cos2A1​×sin2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Combine.

    =sin⁡2Acos⁡2A=tan⁡2A= \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A} = \tan^2 A=cos2Asin2A​=tan2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Second expression

    Start from the second expression.

    (1−tan⁡A1−cot⁡A)2\left(\dfrac{1 - \tan A}{1 - \cot A}\right)^2(1−cotA1−tanA​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Write cot⁡A=1tan⁡A\cot A = \dfrac{1}{\tan A}cotA=tanA1​.

    =(1−tan⁡A1−1tan⁡A)2= \left(\dfrac{1 - \tan A}{1 - \dfrac{1}{\tan A}}\right)^2=​1−tanA1​1−tanA​​2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Combine the bottom: 1−1tan⁡A=tan⁡A−1tan⁡A1 - \dfrac{1}{\tan A} = \dfrac{\tan A - 1}{\tan A}1−tanA1​=tanAtanA−1​.

    =(1−tan⁡A  tan⁡A−1tan⁡A  )2= \left(\dfrac{1 - \tan A}{\;\dfrac{\tan A - 1}{\tan A}\;}\right)^2=​tanAtanA−1​1−tanA​​2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Divide: multiply by the reciprocal.

    =(tan⁡A (1−tan⁡A)tan⁡A−1)2= \left(\dfrac{\tan A\,(1 - \tan A)}{\tan A - 1}\right)^2=(tanA−1tanA(1−tanA)​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    1−tan⁡A=−(tan⁡A−1)1 - \tan A = -(\tan A - 1)1−tanA=−(tanA−1); cancel (tan⁡A−1)(\tan A - 1)(tanA−1).

    =(−tan⁡A)2= (-\tan A)^2=(−tanA)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    A negative number squared is positive.

    =tan⁡2A= \tan^2 A=tan2ASwipe to see the whole equation →

    Conclusion: both expressions equal tan⁡2A\tan^2 Atan2A. Hence proved. (A ≠ 45°, where 1−cot⁡A=01 - \cot A = 01−cotA=0.)

  11. Check: at A = 60°: first =443=3= \dfrac{4}{\dfrac{4}{3}} = 3=34​4​=3; second =(1−31−13)2=(−3)2=3= \left(\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\right)^2 = (-\sqrt{3})^2 = 3=​1−3​1​1−3​​​2=(−3​)2=3; tan⁡260°=3\tan^2 60° = 3tan260°=3 ✔.

    Common trap: Dropping the minus sign in step 9 and worrying that the answer should be −tan⁡2A-\tan^2 A−tan2A. The square makes the sign disappear: (−tan⁡A)2=tan⁡2A(-\tan A)^2 = \tan^2 A(−tanA)2=tan2A.
